Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Understand the importance of national joint registries in implant surveillance.
Understand the origins of arthroplasty registries both in the United States and internationally.
Gain a better understanding of the level of data provided by various registries.
Understand the importance of continued registry use.
Overview of Joint Registries
Background
Registries collect data on implants, surgical techniques, outcomes, and patient-related risk
factors.

Registries may allow for early detection of problems by including a large volume of data from
many patients.

Background
Joint registries exist to collect and disseminate data that may be analyzed to identify
statistically significant findings regarding variables that contribute to the success or
failure of arthroplasty1,2 (Resource 1). This data may include items such as implant data
and patient factors, surgical technique, and implant-associated risk factors.3 Registries
are important because they allow for early detection of problems, minimizing
unnecessary patient suffering and healthcare costs.4,5
The commitment to large-scale efforts to track surgical outcomes can largely be credited
to Ernest A. Codman and the end-result idea that he initially described during the first
half of the 20th century.6 In considering outcomes for commonly performed procedures,
such as hip and knee arthroplasty, national registries serve as the embodiment of this
commitment. As early as 1972, Sir John Charnley recommended the establishment of a
central registry to “put a finger on the pulse of total implant surgery on a nationwide
basis.”7 Early arthroplasty pioneers, such as Charnley and John Insall, insisted on close
and detailed patient follow-up in their own practices to track patients and document
outcomes over time.3 Since the early years of modern arthroplasty, joint registries at the
organizational, regional, national, and even international level have evolved. Currently,
these registries comprise a wide range of data from a large and diverse array of patients
and are serving to shape the future of arthroplasty. In addition, since their inception,
registries have evolved to serve clinical and public health information needs8 (Resource
2).
Registry Levels
Joint registries are assigned a level—from level I to level IV—based on the type of data
collected.


Registry Levels
Although much of the current focus is on national and international registries,
institutional registries have made highly important contributions, and the volume of data
collected by these registries continues to grow.2 Some institutional registries have been
actively collecting data for several decades. One advantage of institutional registries is
the ability to evaluate the performance of specific implants and/or techniques in a
specific setting. The information contained about patients, procedures, complications,
and implant performance in these settings allows for detailed evaluation. This data
collection paradigm—the institutional registry—is referred to as a level IV registry; it
provides highly granular data that allows for comprehensive evaluation of how and why
a procedure or implant failure may occur.3 In contrast, level I registry data includes
patient demographic data; surgeon data; and details of the surgical procedure, including
date, procedure code, and implant-related information. Data in a level II registry includes
patient variables such as comorbidities; body mass index; and perioperative
medications, such as antibiotic prophylaxis. Data in a level III registry includes patient
outcomes and satisfaction scores.9,10
Institutional Joint Registries
Institutional registries have existed in the United States for several decades.
Institutional registries collect data pertaining to the performance of specific implants and/or
surgical techniques in a specific setting.
Mayo Clinic Total Joint Registry

Mayo Clinic Total Joint Registry
The Mayo Clinic Total Joint Registry is the first and largest of these institutional registries
in the United States.11 This registry includes detailed information on more than 100,000
primary and revision hip, knee, shoulder, and elbow replacement procedures performed
at the Mayo Clinic since 1969.3 The registry has facilitated studies in epidemiology, risk
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:49 PM
AAOS | National Joint Registries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001160
3/16

factors, specific surgical techniques, and management of complications that have helped
shape the current practice of total joint arthroplasty.12-15
Harris Joint Registry

Harris Joint Registry
Another institutional registry that has had a major effect on the current practice of
arthroplasty is the Harris Joint Registry. This registry was born out of dissatisfaction with
the lack of rigorous methods by which to evaluate competing surgical strategies in the
late 1950s and early 1960s.3 The registry introduced strict patient data capture and entry
requirements, such that all pertinent preoperative radiographs were collected and each
office visit required obtaining all data for the Harris hip score and a complete set of
radiographs.3 This detailed and meticulous data collection allowed for evaluation of not
only innovations from the Harris Orthopaedic Laboratory but also various other implant
designs, materials, and surgical techniques.16-19
National Registries
Origins of National Registries
National registries have had a major effect on joint replacement surgery around the world.

Origins of National Registries
Compared with institutional registries, national registries provide the benefit of larger
numbers of patients and prosthetic components and may produce more generalizable
data because of the broader diversity of hospitals and surgeons represented3 (Resource
3). These types of registries generally are known as level II registries; they contain
detailed demographic and implant information. With the expansion of longitudinal data
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:49 PM
AAOS | National Joint Registries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001160
4/16

collection and the use of standard patient outcome metrics, these national registries
may become level III registries.3
Many credit the Swedish with developing the first embodiment of a national arthroplasty
register. The Swedish Knee Register was first established in 1976, followed shortly
thereafter by the Swedish Hip Register in 1979.2,20,21 These registries were funded
through the Swedish Medical Research Council and captured data preoperatively and 1,
3, 6, and 10 years postoperatively.3 From the Swedish registries, the arthroplasty
community has gained invaluable knowledge on infection prevention and management,
surgical techniques, and new implant implementation and on the effect of patient
comorbidities on outcomes and patient satisfaction.22-26 The success of the Swedish
registries has been predicated on high levels of surgeon compliance with timely and
accurate data entry by specially trained staff.3
Building on the experiences of the Swedish registries throughout the 1980s and 1990s, a
host of other countries established similar national registries in Europe, Canada,
Australia, and New Zealand.2,27 Many of these country’s registries now belong to the
International Society of Arthroplasty Registries. Currently, the International Society of
Arthroplasty Registries is comprised of 11 full members and 14 associate members and
mandates that full members have obtained participation of more than 80% of national
hospitals with a minimum reporting of 90% of procedures from each reporting
center.2,28
National Joint Registries in the United States
National joint registries have existed in the United States since 2009.
Two major national joint registries in the United States are the American Joint Replacement
Registry (AJRR) and the Function and Outcomes Research for Comparative Effectiveness in
Total Joint Replacement (FORCE-TJR) registry.
American Joint Replacement Registry
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:49 PM
AAOS | National Joint Registries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001160
5/16


American Joint Replacement Registry
In 2009, the AJRR was launched in the United States. The growing impetus to develop this
national registry was outlined by Maloney,29 who reported that the “evidence that a
national joint replacement registry would benefit our patients is strong” and concluded
that the “time has come to initiate such an effort in the United States.” This independent,
not-for-profit registry was supported by the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons
and representatives of providers, consumers, payers, and industry.30 In 2014, the AJRR
released its first annual report, with information from more than 43,000 procedures. By
2016, the annual report covered more than 427,000 procedures from 416 hospitals and
3,170 surgeons.30 Currently, the AJRR collects data from hospitals in all 50 states, and,
despite capturing data from less than one-half of arthroplasty procedures performed
annually in the United States, has compiled information on more than 1 million
procedures.2,3
FORCE-TJR Registry

FORCE-TJR Registry
The FORCE-TJR registry was started in 2010, with funding from the Agency for Healthcare
Research and Quality via a competitive program project award to the University of
Massachusetts Medical School. This registry focused largely on patient-reported
outcomes as the primary outcomes after total joint replacement and on the capture of
quality metrics, such as revision procedures, complications within the first 90 days,
readmissions within the first 30 days, and surgical site infections.8 The FORCE-TJR
registry has been successful in collecting patient-reported outcome measure surveys in a
diverse range of practice settings and contains the largest complete patient-reported
outcome data set in the United States.5
State and Regional Registries
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:49 PM
AAOS | National Joint Registries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001160
6/16


State and Regional Registries
In addition to these national registries, the United States has state and regional
registries, such as the Michigan Arthroplasty Registry Collaborative Quality Initiative, the
California Joint Replacement Registry, and the Kaiser Permanente Total Joint
Replacement Registry.3,8,31
Components of a Successful National Joint Registry
A successful national joint registry has many elements, including funding, infrastructure,
technology, and logistics.
Data quality is imperative for a successful registry.
Data quality has several components, including coverage, completeness, response rate,
missing values, and data validation.

Components of a Successful National Joint Registry
The success of registries depends on multiple factors, including appropriate allocation of
funding, mechanisms for timely review and use of data, and active participation of
surgeons and hospitals.2,30 Many national registries are maintained by national
orthopaedic associations, with funding provided by their respective national
governments.32 In the United States, registries have most successfully been advanced
via multi-stakeholder initiatives, including government, professional society, and
orthopaedic device manufacturers.30 Although the initial operating costs in terms of
infrastructure, technology, and logistical considerations may be high, the cost may be
offset by improvements in quality, such as decreased revision burden, and national
registries may prove to be cost saving in the long term.2,3,29,33
One of the most important factors for success of national or institutional registries is
data quality.32 Malchau et al3 proposed five dimensions of data quality in the setting of a
large registry capturing data from multiple centers, including coverage, completeness,
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:49 PM
AAOS | National Joint Registries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001160
7/16

response rate, missing values, and validation. Coverage references the number of
participating institutions or facilities. Completeness refers to the thoroughness of data
collection and reporting at the individual institution level. Challenges with these factors
may be difficult for registry efforts to overcome. For example, poor response rate among
participants in the Canadian Total Joint Registry has been reported as a major
impediment to data collection in that system.4 Expert consensus has purported that
participation rates should be at least 85% so data is not skewed by unreported revisions
or complications.2 Examples of voluntary and mandatory participation rules exist across
national joint registries, with some authors calling for mandatory reporting as a
necessary prerequisite for establishment of an effective registry.1,32
Response rate must be reported if any type of patient-reported outcome measure
surveys are used, and missing data must be included and accounted for in all statistical
analysis. Validation systems to evaluate and report data integrity also should be used
and reported in a transparent matter.3,21 In addition, compliance among participants is
a necessary component and is predicated on general consensus among the profession
about the importance of the registry, as well as the minimization of registration burden,
the ability of contributors to provide and receive feedback easily, and access to registry
data by participants.3,25,34
Concerns About National Joint Registries
Some concerns have been raised about national joint registries, including publication of data
and surgeon representation.

Concerns About National Joint Registries
Although the benefits of national registries have been extolled in many publications,
surgeons have expressed some reservations regarding the implementation of national
registries. One of the major concerns has been publication of individual hospital and/or
surgeon performance. Such information may have an adverse effect on a surgeon’s
practice and have downstream effects of making surgeons less willing to perform
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:49 PM
AAOS | National Joint Registries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001160
8/16

surgical procedures on higher risk patients.21,34 In addition, some surgeons have
expressed concern that this kind of data may drive patients away from smaller hospitals
and toward major healthcare centers.29 Another concern, particularly with regard to the
National Joint Registry of England, Wales, and Northern Ireland, has been adequate
surgeon representation in registry governance committees.34
Advantages of National Joint Registries
National registries are a powerful surveillance tool.
Registries have allowed for identification of several component-related problems around the
world.
The inclusion of patient-centered outcomes data in national joint registries may be an adjunct
to evaluate quality and to better identify problems.

Advantages of National Joint Registries
National registries have proven to be a powerful tool for surveillance to identify common
and uncommon complications, monitor new surgical techniques and implant technology,
identify problems with implant design or implementation, and reduce patient
morbidity.2 This information may promote best-practice and evidence-based medical
decision making by presenting unbiased information on a large scale.
To date, national registries have largely focused on implant survivorship, identifying
large numbers of arthroplasty procedures with overall low annual failure rates to discern
duration before failure.8 An early example of this was demonstrated by registries in the
United Kingdom in the late 1990s. At that time, before the formation of an
encompassing national registry, the two registries in the United Kingdom were the North
West Regional Arthroplasty Register and the Trent Regional Arthroplasty Study.35,36
Registry data was used to identify a cemented total hip implant associated with a high
rate of femoral component loosening.21,37 Identification of this problem led to issuance
of a hazard notice by the Medical Devices Agency in 1998, with a recommendation that
all patients in whom this device was implanted be contacted and reviewed clinically.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:49 PM
AAOS | National Joint Registries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001160
9/16

Although 4,669 of these prostheses had been supplied to 95 centers in the United
Kingdom, many of the patients could not be identified. The problems faced in identifying
and contacting affected patients in this scenario led the Royal College of Surgeons to
conclude that a national joint registry was necessary to detect problems such as this at
an earlier stage and to help mitigate negative effects.38 Accordingly, the National Joint
Registry of England, Wales, and Northern Ireland was established in 2002, with data
collection beginning in 2003.36
Other examples of national registry data being used to identify problems and facilitate
timely interventions include the response to lipid contamination of Sulzer Orthopedic
components in 2000 and the identification of gender-related failure and increased
revision of hip resurfacing in Australia from approximately 2006 to 2009.1,39-41 In
addition, implementation of data from the Swedish Hip Registry at individual sites has
been purported to have helped reduce Sweden’s national hip arthroplasty revision rate
by more than one-half between 1979 and 1997.42
These and other arthroplasty component and/or technique-related failures may be
minimized via prompt data collection and reporting and illustrate the pressing need for
ongoing registry-level data collection.4 As more and more data become available and the
granularity of that data increases, the opportunity to use registries to examine quality of
care metrics increases. The need for registry-level efforts to track longitudinal patient-
reported outcome measure data has been outlined in several studies.5,28,43 This issue
was brought to light during the large-scale recall of ASR metal-on-metal hip implants in
2010, in which early substantial pain rather that overt implant failure requiring revision
was the first patient-level indicator of a problem.5,44,45 Estimates suggest that as many
as 500,000 patients in the United States received a metal-on-metal hip implant between
2003 and 2010.44 In addition, the increasing focus on patient-centered outcomes is a
reflection of the shifting paradigm from volume-based health care to value-based health
care.28 This level of information has been captured by national registries in countries
such as New Zealand and Sweden since the early 2000s and has been captured more
recently by the National Joint Registry of England, Wales, and Northern Ireland.43,46,47
Similarly, the FORCE-TJR registry database currently collects this data on a national scale
in the United States.5

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001160
10/16

Future Effect of National Joint Registries
National registries will continue to provide important data and may allow for additional
evaluation of outcomes and cost effectiveness on a large scale.
This information may serve to guide surgeons and patients, new medical device development
and implementation, and healthcare policy.

Future Effect of National Joint Registries
The anticipated increase in total joint arthroplasty volume and the use of continuously
evolving technology necessitates the reliable and objective monitoring of national
registries.2,48 In addition, although registries have proven to be valuable in the
identification of problems such as implant failures, complications, and patient-centered
outcomes, they also may be used to evaluate cost effectiveness and identify best
practices. National registries that include patient-level outcomes have a large and not
fully used potential to evaluate economic aspects of total joint arthroplasty, such as cost
and reimbursement.3 They also may provide orthopaedic surgeons, hospital
administrators, and policy makers with valuable information to help inform future
models of post-marketing surveillance of new medical devices, develop evidence-based
healthcare policy, and guide patients and physicians to evidence-based informed clinical
decisions.5
